actions.title: Turn on two-step login for email
actions.whatToDo: Require a code from a phone app every time someone signs in to company email from a new device.
actions.why: Stolen email passwords are behind most payment fraud and many ransomware attacks. A phone code blocks almost all of these break-ins, even when the password is known.
steps: Sign in to your email provider's admin settings with an administrator account.
Find the security settings for two-step verification (also called multi-factor authentication or MFA) and turn it on for all users.
Ask each person to install an authenticator app (such as Microsoft Authenticator or Google Authenticator) and follow the setup prompt on their next sign-in.
Give people a one-week deadline, then make it required for everyone, including owners and managers.

m365: Go to entra.microsoft.com and sign in with your Microsoft 365 admin account.
Open Identity, then Overview, then Properties, and select 'Manage security defaults'. Set Security defaults to Enabled and save.
Tell staff that on their next sign-in they will be asked to install the Microsoft Authenticator app and scan a code. It takes about 5 minutes each.
Check the next day in the admin center (Users, then Active users, then Multi-factor authentication) that everyone has registered.
Keep one emergency 'break glass' admin account with a long password stored somewhere safe, in case a phone is lost.
google: Go to admin.google.com and sign in with your Google Workspace admin account.
Open Security, then Authentication, then 2-step verification. Check 'Allow users to turn on 2-step verification'.
Ask staff to turn it on at myaccount.google.com/security using the Google Authenticator app or a phone prompt.
After one week, return to the same admin page and set Enforcement to 'On' so it is required for everyone.
Keep backup codes for the admin account in a safe place, in case a phone is lost.

actions.title: Turn on two-step login for banking, accounting, and portals
actions.whatToDo: Switch on phone codes for online banking, accounting software, load boards, and fleet or TMS portals.
actions.why: These are the accounts where money and loads move. Criminals who get in can redirect payments or steal loads, and a phone code stops most of them.
steps: Make a list of every online tool that touches money or loads: online banking, accounting (QuickBooks, Sage, Xero), load boards, fleet telematics, and TMS portals.
For each one, sign in and look under Security or Account settings for 'two-step', '2FA', or 'multi-factor'. Turn it on.
Use an authenticator app rather than text messages where the tool allows it.
For tools that do not offer it, ask the vendor when it is coming, and use a unique strong password in the meantime.
Tick each one off your list so you know nothing was missed.

actions.title: Give everyone their own login and stop sharing accounts
actions.whatToDo: Replace shared logins and shared tablets with a personal login for each person, protected with a PIN.
actions.why: With shared accounts you cannot tell who did what, and you cannot cut off one person without disrupting everyone. Personal logins fix both.
steps: List every shared login in use: dispatch or load board accounts, shared email inboxes, shared tablets in trucks or on the floor.
Check whether each tool allows extra users. Many load boards and TMS tools include extra seats or charge a small amount per user.
Create a named account for each person, and use shared mailboxes (not shared passwords) for team inboxes.
Set a PIN on every work phone and tablet and turn on remote wipe through your email provider's device settings.
Change the old shared password once everyone has moved over, so it no longer works.

m365: Go to admin.microsoft.com and sign in with your Microsoft 365 admin account.
Under Users, then Active users, select 'Add a user' for each person who currently shares a login.
Create a shared mailbox instead of a shared password: go to Teams & groups, then Shared mailboxes, then 'Add a shared mailbox' for team inboxes.
Enroll phones and tablets in mobile device management (Devices, then Enrollment) to require a PIN and allow remote wipe.
Once everyone has moved over, change the old shared password so it no longer works.
google: Go to admin.google.com and sign in with your Google Workspace admin account.
Under Directory, then Users, select 'Add new user' for each person who currently shares a login.
Create a Google Group with a collaborative inbox instead of a shared password: go to Groups, then 'Create group', then turn on 'Collaborative Inbox' under access settings.
Enroll phones and tablets under Devices, then Mobile & endpoints, to require a PIN and allow remote wipe.
Once everyone has moved over, change the old shared password so it no longer works.

actions.title: Create an offboarding checklist
actions.whatToDo: Write a one-page checklist of every system and vendor with access, and use it the same day anyone leaves.
actions.why: Forgotten accounts of former staff and old vendors are an easy way in. A checklist makes removing access fast and routine.
steps: Start a simple document or spreadsheet listing every system people log into: email, banking, accounting, load boards, telematics, door codes, and Wi-Fi.
Add every outside vendor or IT provider that can access your systems, with a contact name for each.
When someone leaves, go down the list that same day: disable accounts, collect devices, and change any shared passwords they knew.
Review the vendor list every six months and remove anyone you no longer work with.

m365: In your checklist, note that access is cut in admin.microsoft.com under Users, then Active users: select the person and choose 'Block sign-in'.
From the same page, reset their password and remove them from Microsoft 365 groups and Teams.
Add every outside vendor or IT provider with delegated admin access (Settings, then Partner relationships) to the list with a contact name.
When someone leaves, block sign-in and reset their password that same day, then reassign or remove their mailbox once their files are backed up.
Review the vendor and partner access list every six months and remove anyone you no longer work with.
google: In your checklist, note that access is cut in admin.google.com under Directory, then Users: select the person and choose 'Suspend user'.
From the same page, reset their password and remove them from Google Groups; use the data transfer tool if you need to move their Drive files first.
Add every outside vendor or IT provider with an admin role (Account, then Admin roles) to the list with a contact name.
When someone leaves, suspend the account that same day, then delete it once their files and email are transferred or backed up.
Review the vendor and admin role list every six months and remove anyone you no longer work with.

actions.title: Set up a company password manager
actions.whatToDo: Give staff a password manager so every account gets its own strong password without anyone needing to remember them.
actions.why: Reused and written-down passwords are how one breach turns into many. A password manager makes the safe option the easy option.
steps: Pick a business password manager (for example Bitwarden, 1Password, or Keeper). Business plans cost a few dollars per user per month.
Set it up for the owner and office manager first, and move the most important passwords in: banking, email admin, and accounting.
Invite the rest of the team and show them how to save and fill passwords in a 15-minute huddle.
Use shared folders for team logins instead of passing passwords around by text or sticky note.

actions.title: Remove admin rights from everyday accounts
actions.whatToDo: Make sure day-to-day computer accounts are standard users, with admin rights kept to one or two people.
actions.why: If an everyday account is an admin, one bad click lets ransomware install itself and spread. Standard accounts contain the damage.
steps: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Accounts, then Other users, and check which accounts are 'Administrator'.
Change everyday accounts to 'Standard user'.
Keep a separate admin account for the one or two people who install software, and use it only when needed.
If you use Microsoft 365 or Google admin roles, check that only one or two people hold the top admin role.

m365: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Accounts, then Other users, and check which accounts are 'Administrator'. Change everyday accounts to 'Standard user'.
Keep a separate local admin account for the one or two people who install software, and use it only when needed.
Go to entra.microsoft.com, open Identity, then Roles & admins, then 'Global Administrator', and confirm only one or two trusted people are assigned.
Turn on Security defaults (Identity, then Overview, then Properties) so anyone with an admin role must use MFA.
google: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Accounts, then Other users, and check which accounts are 'Administrator'. Change everyday accounts to 'Standard user'.
Keep a separate local admin account for the one or two people who install software, and use it only when needed.
Go to admin.google.com, open Account, then Admin roles, then 'Super Admin', and confirm only one or two trusted people are assigned.
Turn on 2-step verification enforcement for anyone holding an admin role (Security, then Authentication, then 2-step verification).

actions.title: Adopt a call-back rule for any bank detail change
actions.whatToDo: Never change a supplier's, carrier's, or grower's bank details without calling them at a number you already had on file, and require a second approval for large payments.
actions.why: Fake 'we changed banks' emails are the most common way small businesses lose money to fraud. A quick phone call to a trusted number stops it, at no cost.
steps: Write the rule down in one sentence: 'We only change bank details after calling the company at a number we already had on file.'
Never use the phone number in the email asking for the change. Use your records, the contract, or their public website.
Set a dollar limit (for example $5,000) above which a second person must approve the payment.
Tell everyone who handles payments today, and post the rule next to the accounting computer.
If a request feels rushed or secretive, treat that as a warning sign and slow down.

actions.title: Run a 30-minute fake email awareness session
actions.whatToDo: Walk staff through real examples of fake emails and turn on an 'External sender' warning in email.
actions.why: Most attacks start with an email. A short, practical session makes people much more likely to pause before clicking or paying.
steps: Book 30 minutes with office staff and dispatchers. Use the free Get Cyber Safe materials from the Government of Canada as a guide.
Show 3 or 4 real examples: a fake invoice, a fake 'boss' asking for gift cards, a fake load board login page.
Agree on one simple rule: if unsure, forward it to one named person before clicking or paying.
Turn on an 'External' banner for emails from outside the company in your email admin settings.
Repeat a short refresher every year and whenever a new person joins.

m365: Book 30 minutes with office staff and dispatchers. Use the free Get Cyber Safe materials from the Government of Canada as a guide.
Show 3 or 4 real examples: a fake invoice, a fake 'boss' asking for gift cards, a fake load board login page.
Agree on one simple rule: if unsure, forward it to one named person before clicking or paying.

Turn on the external sender tag: an admin runs 'Set-ExternalInOutlook -Enabled $true' in Exchange Online PowerShell, or adds a mail flow rule in the Exchange admin center that prepends '[EXTERNAL]' to outside emails.
Repeat a short refresher every year and whenever a new person joins.
google: Book 30 minutes with office staff and dispatchers. Use the free Get Cyber Safe materials from the Government of Canada as a guide.
Show 3 or 4 real examples: a fake invoice, a fake 'boss' asking for gift cards, a fake load board login page.
Agree on one simple rule: if unsure, forward it to one named person before clicking or paying.
In admin.google.com open Apps, then Google Workspace, then Gmail, then End User Access, and turn on 'Warn for external recipients'. Also check Safety settings for spoofing protection.
Repeat a short refresher every year and whenever a new person joins.

actions.title: Turn on DMARC for your email domain
actions.whatToDo: Publish SPF and DMARC records for your domain so other companies' email systems can block emails faking your name.
actions.why: Without DMARC, anyone can send email that looks like it came from you, including fake invoices to your own customers. It is free to set up.
steps: Log in to wherever your domain is registered (for example GoDaddy, Namecheap, or your web host) and open the DNS settings.
Make sure you have an SPF record (a TXT record starting with 'v=spf1') that lists your email provider.
Add a TXT record named '_dmarc' with the value 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourdomain.ca' to start collecting reports.
After 2 to 4 weeks with no problems, change 'p=none' to 'p=quarantine', and later to 'p=reject'.
Run the domain check in this tool again to confirm it is working.

m365: Log in to wherever your domain is registered (for example GoDaddy, Namecheap, or your web host) and open the DNS settings.
Check you have an SPF TXT record: 'v=spf1 include:spf.protection.outlook.com -all'.
In the Microsoft Defender portal (security.microsoft.com), open Email authentication settings, then DKIM, and turn on DKIM signing for your domain.
Add a TXT record named '_dmarc' with the value 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourdomain.ca'. After 2 to 4 weeks with no problems, change to 'p=quarantine', then 'p=reject'.
Run the domain check in this tool again to confirm it is working.
google: Log in to wherever your domain is registered (for example GoDaddy, Namecheap, or Google Domains / Squarespace) and open the DNS settings.
Check you have an SPF TXT record: 'v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all'.
In admin.google.com open Apps, then Google Workspace, then Gmail, then Authenticate email, and turn on DKIM.
Add a TXT record named '_dmarc' with the value 'v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:you@yourdomain.ca'. After 2 to 4 weeks with no problems, change to 'p=quarantine', then 'p=reject'.
Run the domain check in this tool again to confirm it is working.

actions.title: Turn on automatic updates and antivirus everywhere
actions.whatToDo: Make sure every computer installs security updates on its own and has Microsoft Defender or another antivirus switched on.
actions.why: Most ransomware uses holes that already have a fix. Automatic updates and built-in antivirus block the bulk of everyday attacks for free.
steps: On each Windows computer, open Settings, then Windows Update, and make sure updates are on and not paused. Set active hours so restarts happen overnight.
Open Windows Security and check that Virus and threat protection shows green.
Turn on automatic updates for web browsers and common apps like Adobe Reader and Office.
Replace any computer running Windows 10 or older that can no longer receive updates.
Put a reminder on the calendar to spot-check every computer once a month.

actions.title: Set up automatic backups with one offline copy and test a restore
actions.whatToDo: Back up important data automatically, keep one copy disconnected or separate from your network, and prove you can restore it.
actions.why: Backups are what let you recover from ransomware without paying. But ransomware also hunts for backups it can reach, so one copy must be out of reach.
steps: List what you cannot lose: accounting files, dispatch and load records, driver logs, customer lists, and email.
Set up an automatic daily backup to a cloud backup service (for example Backblaze, Acronis, or your IT provider's service) that keeps older versions.
Keep a second copy that is offline or separate: a drive you unplug and take off-site each week, or a cloud backup with 'immutable' or locked copies.
Once a quarter, pick a file or folder and actually restore it to prove the backup works.
Write down where the backups are and how to restore them, and keep it with your incident plan.

m365: List what you cannot lose: accounting files, dispatch and load records, driver logs, customer lists, and email.
If you use SharePoint, OneDrive, or Exchange Online, turn on Microsoft 365 Backup (search 'Backup' in admin.microsoft.com) to keep restorable copies of your files and mailboxes.

Also keep a second, separate copy offline or with a third-party cloud backup service that supports 'immutable' or locked copies. The default recycle bin and version history are not enough on their own.
Once a quarter, restore a file or mailbox item to prove the backup works.
Write down where the backups are and how to restore them, and keep it with your incident plan.
google: List what you cannot lose: accounting files, dispatch and load records, driver logs, customer lists, and email.

If you use Google Drive or Gmail, turn on Google Vault (admin.google.com, then Apps, then Google Workspace, then Vault) so files and email can be retained and recovered through vault.google.com. Also check Drive's version history and trash retention.
Also keep a second, separate copy offline or with a third-party cloud backup service that supports 'immutable' or locked copies. Vault and Drive's built-in history are not enough on their own.
Once a quarter, restore a file or email to prove the backup works.
Write down where the backups are and how to restore them, and keep it with your incident plan.

actions.title: Lock down remote access to the office
actions.whatToDo: Replace any open remote desktop connection with a secure remote access tool that requires a phone code.
actions.why: Remote desktop left open to the internet is one of the top ways ransomware gangs break in. Closing it removes a major door.
steps: Ask whoever set up your network (or your IT provider) whether any computer has remote desktop (RDP, port 3389) open to the internet.
Close those openings on the router or firewall.
Use a secure remote access option with a phone code instead: a business VPN, or a remote access service with two-step login turned on.
Keep a list of who is allowed to connect from outside, and remove people when they leave.

actions.title: Turn off always-on vendor remote access to equipment
actions.whatToDo: Switch off TeamViewer, AnyDesk, or similar tools on equipment computers, and only turn them on when the vendor actually needs to connect.
actions.why: Always-on remote access is an open door to your refrigeration and equipment. If the vendor or their password is compromised, attackers can walk straight in.
steps: Walk around and find every computer or controller that runs TeamViewer, AnyDesk, or a similar remote tool, especially refrigeration and monitoring systems.
Set the tool so it does not start automatically, or uninstall it and reinstall only when needed.
Agree with each vendor: they call you first, you turn access on, and you turn it off when they are done.
Change the remote access password and turn on two-step login in the tool if it offers it.
Add each vendor to your vendor access list.

actions.title: Separate equipment and guest Wi-Fi from office network
actions.whatToDo: Put connected equipment and guest or driver Wi-Fi on their own networks, separate from office computers.
actions.why: Separate networks stop a problem in one place from spreading everywhere. An infected office computer should not be able to reach your refrigeration controls.
steps: Draw a simple map of what is connected: office computers, equipment and sensors, cameras, and guest or driver Wi-Fi.
Ask your IT provider or router supplier to create separate networks (VLANs) for equipment and for guests. Many business routers can do this.
Turn on the guest network option on your Wi-Fi and give drivers and visitors that password only.
Test that equipment still reports properly and that guests cannot see office computers.

actions.title: Change default passwords on routers, cameras, and equipment
actions.whatToDo: Replace every factory password on routers, cameras, controllers, and sensors with a unique strong one.
actions.why: Default passwords are published online, and automated tools scan the internet for devices still using them.
steps: List every networked device: routers, Wi-Fi access points, cameras and recorders, refrigeration controllers, sensors, and printers.
Log in to each one and change the admin password to a unique strong one. Store them in your password manager.
While you are there, check for a firmware update and install it.
If a device will not let you change its password, ask the vendor about a replacement or keep it off the internet.

actions.title: Add breach notification to vendor contracts
actions.whatToDo: Ask vendors with access to your systems to commit, in writing, to telling you quickly if they are breached.
actions.why: If a trusted vendor is compromised, you need to know fast so you can cut off their access before attackers use it against you.
steps: Start with your most important vendors: IT provider, refrigeration or equipment vendor, TMS or dispatch software, and payroll.
Send each a short request to add a clause saying they will notify you within 72 hours of any security incident that could affect you.
Add the same clause to your standard template for new vendor contracts.
Record who agreed on your vendor access list.

actions.title: Write a one-page "if we're compromised" plan
actions.whatToDo: Write one page that says who to call and what to do first if you are hit by ransomware or payment fraud.
actions.why: A plan does not stop attacks, but it makes every attack less damaging. In a crisis, the first few hours decide how bad it gets.
steps: List who to call: your IT provider, your bank's fraud line, your insurer, and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (1-833-CYBER-88).
Write the first three steps for ransomware: unplug affected computers from the network, do not pay or respond, call your IT provider.
Write the first three steps for payment fraud: call your bank immediately to recall the payment, report to local police and the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre, warn the affected partner.
Note how to tell your key customers if their shipments or data could be affected.
Print it and keep a copy somewhere that does not need a computer to reach.

actions.title: Get a cyber insurance quote
actions.whatToDo: Ask your broker for a cyber insurance quote that covers ransomware, payment fraud, and incident response help.
actions.why: Insurance helps cover recovery costs and usually includes expert help on the day. Many insurers also give discounts for the fixes on this list.
steps: Call your current business insurance broker and ask about cyber coverage.
Ask specifically whether it covers ransomware, funds transfer fraud (social engineering), and business interruption.
Have the answers from this check-up ready. Insurers will ask about two-step login, backups, and training.
Compare at least two quotes and check the incident response hotline is included.

actions.title: Lock down load changes: call back and get a second OK
actions.whatToDo: Any change to a pickup or delivery address is confirmed by calling the broker or shipper at a number you already had, and a second person OKs it before the driver is told.
actions.why: Load theft by email works because one busy person can reroute a truck on the strength of a single message. A call to a known number and a second pair of eyes stops it, and it costs nothing.
steps: Write the rule down in one sentence: 'No pickup or delivery change goes to a driver until we've called the broker or shipper back on a number we already had, and a second person has OK'd it.'
Never use the phone number or link in the email asking for the change. Use the rate confirmation, your TMS, or the company's public website.
Pick who can give the second OK on each shift (for example, the dispatch lead or the owner) and make sure one of them is always reachable.
Watch for pressure: last-minute changes, a new consignee, 'urgent' wording, or a slightly different email address. Treat these as reasons to slow down.
Tell every dispatcher today, post the rule by the dispatch desk, and log each change with who called and who approved.

cccs.source: Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, Baseline Cyber Security Controls for Small and Medium Organizations, V1.2 (February 2020)

rules.label: Losses start in under 4 hours of downtime
Losses start within 4 to 24 hours of downtime
Business can run for more than 3 days without computers
Top 3 customers are more than half of revenue
Sends or receives bank transfers every week
Stores SINs, banking details, or payment info
51 or more people to manage logins for

profile.why: Different kinds of businesses get targeted in different ways. Freight brokers see far more payment fraud; cold storage sites rely more on connected equipment.
More people means more logins to manage, and more chances for a shared or forgotten account.

profile.text: If your computers stopped working, how long before you start losing serious money?
profile.why: This tells us how badly an outage like ransomware would hurt. The faster the losses start, the higher the impact.

profile.text: Do you handle perishable goods (food, livestock, or temperature-sensitive cargo)?
profile.why: When goods can spoil, even a short disruption turns into real losses for you and your customers.

profile.text: Do your top 3 customers make up more than half your revenue?
profile.why: If a few big customers matter most, an incident that affects them, or a failed security audit, could hit you hard.

profile.text: Do you send or receive bank transfers to suppliers, carriers, or growers every week?
profile.why: Regular transfers are exactly what payment fraud criminals look for. They try to slip their own bank details into a routine payment.

profile.text: Do you store employee SINs, banking details, or customer payment info?
profile.why: Losing or leaking this kind of information can bring legal duties, notification costs, and lost trust.

profile.text: Do you have equipment connected to the internet, like refrigeration monitoring, grain systems, sensors, or cameras?
profile.why: Connected equipment can be reached from outside. If you are not sure, we will assume yes so we do not miss a risk.

profile.text: What do you use for email?
profile.why: We use this to give you step-by-step instructions for the system you actually have. The domain check on the next screen can fill this in for you.

prompts.intro: There are no wrong answers. Honest answers get you better advice. If you're not sure, tap "Not sure" and we'll add it to your list to check.

prompts.title: Do you need a code from your phone to log in?
prompts.why: This is called two-step login. Even if someone steals a password, they can't get in without the code from your phone. Email matters most because password resets go there, and your money and load tools are what criminals want.

labelBySector.carrier: If a broker or shipper emails to change a pickup or delivery address, can one dispatcher make the change on their own?
labelBySector.broker: If a shipper or carrier emails to change a pickup or delivery address, can one person make the change on their own?

options.label: No, we call back on a known number and a second person OKs it
We call back, but one person can still change it
Yes, one person can change it from the email

prompts.title: Email
prompts.why: Most attacks start with an email. Short training helps people pause before clicking. An "External" label shows when a message claiming to be from your boss came from outside. DMARC stops strangers sending email that looks like it came from your company, such as fake invoices to your customers.

rows.question: Q9
rows.label: Has your team had any training on spotting fake emails in the past year?

rows.question: Q10
rows.label: Do emails from outside the company show a warning label?

rows.question: Q11
rows.label: Is your email domain protected against spoofing (DMARC)?
rows.labelBasic: Is your company email set up so strangers can't send fake emails that look like they came from you? (The email check can answer this.)

prompts.title: Computers, phones, and tablets
prompts.why: Attackers use known holes in old software, and automatic updates close them. Built-in antivirus like Microsoft Defender blocks most common malware, but only if it's on. A lost phone or truck tablet can hold email and saved passwords.

rows.question: Q12
rows.label: Do computers install security updates automatically?

rows.question: Q13
rows.label: Is antivirus (like Microsoft Defender) turned on?

rows.question: Q16
rows.label: Are work phones and tablets locked with a PIN, and can you wipe them remotely if they're lost?

options.label: Only one of these, or only some devices

rows.na: We don't use phones or tablets for work

prompts.title: How are your files and business data backed up?
prompts.why: Backups let you recover from ransomware or a dead hard drive without paying anyone. Ransomware hunts for backups it can reach, so the copy that saves you is one that's offline or separate, and that you've actually restored from.

options.label: Now and then, when someone remembers
Regularly, but only one copy, and we've never tried restoring it
Regularly, plus either an offline copy or a restore we've tested (not both)
Regularly, with an offline or separate copy we've restored from

prompts.title: Connecting from outside the office
prompts.why: Remote desktop left open to the internet is one of the top ways ransomware gangs get in. A secure connection that also needs a phone code closes that door.

rows.question: Q17
rows.label: When people connect to office computers from home or on the road, how do they do it?

options.label: A secure connection that needs a phone code
A secure connection, but no phone code
Remote desktop or a remote tool with just a password

rows.na: Nobody connects from outside the office

prompts.title: Equipment, routers, and Wi-Fi
prompts.why: Always-on vendor remote access is an open door to your equipment. A separate network keeps an infected office computer away from refrigeration or sensors. Factory passwords like "admin" are published online. Visitors' and drivers' phones shouldn't share a network with your business computers.

rows.question: Q18
rows.label: Is vendor remote access to your equipment (TeamViewer, AnyDesk) switched off when it's not being used?

rows.question: Q19
rows.label: Is your connected equipment on a separate network from office computers?
rows.labelBasic: Are fridges, sensors, and cameras on a separate Wi-Fi or network from your office computers?

rows.question: Q20
rows.label: Have the default passwords been changed on routers, cameras, and equipment?

rows.question: Q21
rows.label: Is guest or driver Wi-Fi separate from your business network?

prompts.title: Vendors and IT providers
prompts.why: You can't protect a door you don't know about, so keep a list of who can get into your systems. If a vendor is compromised and doesn't tell you, attackers can use that access for weeks.

rows.question: Q22
rows.label: Do you keep a list of every vendor or IT provider that can access your systems?

options.label: Yes, and it's up to date

rows.question: Q23
rows.label: Do your contracts require vendors to tell you if they're compromised?

prompts.title: If something goes wrong
prompts.why: These don't stop an attack, but they make every attack less damaging. A one-page plan saves hours of panic. Cyber insurance helps pay for recovery and often includes expert help on the day.

rows.question: Q24
rows.label: Do you have a written list of who to call and what to do if your business is compromised?

rows.question: Q25
rows.label: Do you have cyber insurance?

options.label: Some cover, but not sure it includes cyber attacks

sections.title: Logins and accounts
sections.intro: How people sign in to your computers and online tools.

sections.title: Payments, loads, and email
sections.intro: How you protect payments and shipments, and spot fake emails.

sections.title: Computers and backups
sections.intro: Keeping computers healthy and your data recoverable.

sections.title: Equipment and remote access
sections.intro: Connected equipment, Wi-Fi, and connecting from outside the office.

sections.title: Vendors and planning

questions.text: Do you need a code from your phone (or an app) to log into company email?
questions.why: This is often called two-step login or multi-factor authentication. Even if someone steals a password, they cannot get in without the code from your phone. Email is the key to everything else, because password resets go there.
questions.tech: MFA on email (Entra ID / Google 2-Step Verification)

questions.text: Do your other online tools (banking, accounting, load boards, fleet or TMS portals) require a phone code to log in?
questions.why: Criminals target the tools where money and loads move. A phone code on each one stops most stolen-password break-ins.
questions.gapLabel: No phone code on business portals
questions.mappingNote: BC.5.1 names financial accounts explicitly. Cloud portals and online banking are externally-exposed applications under CIS 6.3.
questions.tech: MFA on SaaS: banking, accounting, load boards, TMS

questions.text: Does every person have their own login, with no shared accounts or shared tablets?
questions.why: With a shared login you cannot tell who did what, and you cannot remove one person's access without changing it for everyone.
questions.mappingNote: Neither framework has a standalone 'no shared accounts' rule. Individual logins are what make least privilege (BC.12.1), removing one person's access (BC.12.3), and a per-person account inventory (CIS 5.1) possible.
questions.tech: Unique user accounts, no shared credentials

questions.text: When someone leaves, is their access removed the same day?
questions.why: Former staff accounts that stay active are a common way in, whether used by the former employee or by someone who stole the password.
questions.tech: Same-day deprovisioning for leavers

questions.text: Do staff use a password manager instead of reusing or writing down passwords?
questions.why: When one website is breached, criminals try the same password everywhere else. A password manager makes it easy to use a different strong password for each site.
questions.mappingNote: A password manager is the practical way to meet CIS 5.2 (unique passwords). 5.2 also sets length minimums this question does not ask about.
questions.tech: Password manager, no credential reuse

questions.text: Are admin rights on computers limited to one or two trusted people?
questions.why: If everyday accounts have admin rights, one bad click can let ransomware take over the whole computer and spread.
questions.mappingNote: CIS 5.4 requires dedicated admin accounts, which the recommended fix sets up, but the question only asks how many people hold admin rights.
questions.tech: Least privilege: no local admin on daily accounts

questions.text: Before changing a supplier's or carrier's bank details, do you call them at a number you already had on file to confirm?
questions.why: Most payment fraud starts with an email saying 'we changed banks.' Calling a number you already trust, not the one in the email, stops it cold.
questions.gapLabel: No call-back rule for bank changes
questions.mappingNote: A call-back rule is a payment procedure, not a baseline IT control. CCCS BC.6.1 and CIS 14.2 cover training staff to recognize business email compromise, but neither requires verifying bank changes. Shown separately on the Supplier Security Summary.
questions.tech: Out-of-band verification of payee bank changes

questions.text: Do large payments need approval from a second person?
questions.why: A second set of eyes catches rushed or unusual payment requests, which is exactly what fraudsters rely on.
questions.gapLabel: No second approval on large payments
questions.mappingNote: Dual approval of payments is a financial control. CCCS BC.12 and CIS Control 6 cover access to IT systems, not payment approval. Shown separately on the Supplier Security Summary.
questions.tech: Dual authorization above a payment threshold

questions.text: Has staff had any training on spotting fake emails in the past year?
questions.why: Most attacks start with an email. A short session on what fake emails look like makes people far more likely to pause before clicking.
questions.tech: Phishing awareness training, at least yearly

questions.text: Does your email show a warning on messages from outside the company?
questions.why: A simple 'External sender' banner helps staff notice when an email claiming to be from the boss actually came from outside.
questions.mappingNote: External-sender tagging is an email gateway rule, closest to BC.9.8 (email filtering). No CIS v8.1 safeguard covers it: Control 9 addresses browsers, DNS filtering, DMARC, file types, and email anti-malware.
questions.tech: External-sender banner on inbound mail

questions.text: Is your email domain protected against spoofing (DMARC)?
questions.why: Without this setting, anyone in the world can send an email that looks like it came from your company, for example a fake invoice to your customers. DMARC tells other email systems to block those fakes. The domain check can answer this for you.
questions.tech: DMARC at p=quarantine or p=reject

questions.text: Do computers install security updates automatically?
questions.why: Attackers use known holes in old software. Automatic updates close those holes without anyone having to remember.
questions.mappingNote: Fully covers operating system updates (7.3); application updates (7.4) only partly.
questions.tech: Automatic OS and application patching

questions.text: Does every computer have antivirus or Microsoft Defender turned on?
questions.why: Built-in tools like Microsoft Defender are free and block most common malware, but only if they are switched on.
questions.mappingNote: CIS 10.2 (automatic signature updates) is on by default in Microsoft Defender, but the question does not ask about it directly.
questions.tech: Endpoint protection (AV/EDR) on every device

questions.text: Do you back up important files and business data regularly?
questions.why: Backups are what let you recover from ransomware, a dead hard drive, or an accidental delete without paying anyone.
questions.mappingNote: Asks whether backups are regular, not whether they are automated or proven to restore. Q15 covers the rest.
questions.tech: Scheduled backups

questions.text: Is at least one backup kept offline or separate from your network, and have you tested restoring it?
questions.why: Ransomware looks for backups it can reach and locks them too. A copy that is disconnected, and that you know actually restores, is your safety net.
questions.mappingNote: BC.7.2 also requires encrypted backups, which is not asked.
questions.tech: Offline or immutable backup, with a tested restore

questions.topic: PIN and remote wipe on phones
questions.text: Are phones and tablets used for work locked with a PIN, and can you wipe them remotely if lost?
questions.why: A lost phone or truck tablet can hold email, load details, and saved passwords. A PIN and remote wipe keep that information safe.
questions.mappingNote: On modern phones a PIN is what protects the device's encrypted storage (BC.8.4). Remote wipe usually comes from a mobility management tool (BC.8.5). The other five BC.8 requirements are not asked.
questions.tech: MDM: device passcode and remote wipe

questions.text: If people connect to office computers from home, is it through a secure method with a phone code (not open remote desktop)?
questions.why: Remote desktop left open to the internet is one of the top ways ransomware gangs get in. A secure connection with a phone code closes that door.
questions.mappingNote: The phone-code part also supports BC.5.1. CIS 12.7 (VPN plus central authentication) is an IG2 safeguard and only partly covered.
questions.tech: VPN or ZTNA with MFA, no internet-exposed RDP

questions.topic: Vendor remote access off when idle
questions.text: Is vendor remote access to your equipment (for example TeamViewer or AnyDesk) turned off when not in use?
questions.why: Always-on remote access tools are an open door. If the vendor is compromised, or the password leaks, someone can reach your equipment directly.
questions.mappingNote: Neither framework names vendor remote-access tools. One left running when unused is an unnecessary feature or service (BC.4.1, CIS 4.8) and part of how an outside provider accesses your systems (BC.10.2).
questions.tech: Just-in-time vendor remote access (TeamViewer, AnyDesk)

questions.text: Is your equipment on a separate network from office computers?
questions.why: If an office computer gets infected, a separate network keeps the problem from spreading to refrigeration, sensors, or cameras, and the other way around.
questions.mappingNote: CCCS has no general network segmentation requirement. It applies the same isolation idea to internet-facing servers (BC.9.1) and point-of-sale systems (BC.9.6), so this counts toward BC.9 without claiming either. CIS 12.2 requires segmentation (IG2).
questions.tech: OT/IoT network segmentation

questions.text: Have default passwords been changed on routers, cameras, and equipment?
questions.why: Factory passwords like 'admin' are published online. Attackers scan the internet for devices that still use them.
questions.tech: Default credentials changed on network and IoT devices

questions.text: Is guest or driver Wi-Fi separate from your business network?
questions.why: Visitors' and drivers' phones can carry malware. A separate guest network keeps them away from your business computers.
questions.mappingNote: Guest and driver Wi-Fi is a public network under BC.9.5. CIS v8.1 has no guest Wi-Fi safeguard; it falls under segmentation in 12.2.
questions.tech: Guest Wi-Fi isolated from the business network

questions.text: Do you have a list of every vendor or IT provider that can access your systems?
questions.why: You cannot protect a door you do not know about. A simple list lets you check and remove access when a vendor relationship ends.
questions.mappingNote: CCCS does not require a vendor inventory, but you cannot evaluate how providers access your systems (BC.10.2) without one.
questions.tech: Third-party access inventory

questions.text: Do your contracts require vendors to tell you if they are breached?
questions.why: If a vendor is compromised and does not tell you, attackers can use that access for weeks before you notice.
questions.gapLabel: No vendor breach notice in contracts
questions.mappingNote: CIS 15.4 lists incident and data breach notification as an example contract requirement.
questions.tech: Breach-notification clause in vendor contracts

questions.text: Do you have a written list of who to call and what to do if your business is compromised?
questions.why: This does not stop an attack, but it makes every attack less damaging. In a crisis, a one-page plan saves hours of panic and costly mistakes.
questions.gapLabel: No plan for if we're compromised
questions.mappingNote: A written contact list and first steps meet CIS 17.2 directly. Naming who is in charge (17.1) and a full response process (17.4) are only partly covered.
questions.tech: Written incident response plan and contact list

questions.text: Do you have cyber insurance?
questions.why: Cyber insurance helps cover the cost of recovering from ransomware or payment fraud, and often includes expert help on the day it happens.
questions.mappingNote: CIS 17.2 lists your insurer as an incident contact but does not ask whether you have cyber insurance.
questions.tech: Cyber insurance, including social-engineering fraud cover

questions.text: If someone asks to change a pickup or delivery address, does that need a call-back to a number on file and a second person's OK?
questions.why: Criminals who get into an email account, or fake a broker's email, send a 'new delivery address' and count on one busy person changing it. A call to a number you already had, plus a second person's OK, keeps the load out of their hands.
questions.gapLabel: One person can change where a load goes
questions.mappingNote: Confirming shipment changes is an operational procedure. Neither the CCCS baseline nor the CIS Controls cover it. Shown with the payment and shipment safeguards on the Supplier Security Summary.
questions.tech: Out-of-band verification and dual control on shipment changes

effort.label: Effort only
effort.description: Most risk removed for the work involved. Cost is shown but not counted.

cost.label: Effort + cost
cost.description: Cost counts as extra effort, so a free fix beats a paid one that does the same good. Essential recovery fixes are exempt from the cost penalty.
cost.formula: risk reduction ÷ (effort + cost weight × cost points)

essential.description: A fix is essential when it resolves a CIS Implementation Group 1 safeguard in one of these recovery and response controls. Essential fixes skip the cost penalty and are scheduled no later than latestTimeframe days.

cisControls.11: Lets you recover your data after ransomware or a failure, without paying.
cisControls.17: Limits the damage and downtime when an attack gets through.

rules.title: Load change rule
rules.lead: No pickup or delivery address changes until BOTH of these are done:
must: We call the broker or shipper back on a number we already have (from the rate confirmation or our records). Never the number or link in the email.
A second person OKs the change before the driver is told.
warnings: An email address that is slightly different

rules.title: Bank details change rule
rules.lead: Nobody changes a supplier's, carrier's, or customer's bank details until BOTH of these are done:
must: We call the company back on a number we already had on file. Never the number in the email asking for the change.
A second person approves any large payment to the new details.
warnings: A request to pay before the usual date
Pressure to keep it quiet or rush it
An email address that is slightly different

rules.title: If we're compromised: who to call
rules.lead: If a computer is locked, money goes missing, or an email account is taken over, stay calm and work down this list:
must: Unplug the affected computer from the network (pull the cable or turn off Wi-Fi). Do not turn it off.
If money was sent, call the bank right away. Speed matters for getting it back.
Call the people below, then tell customers whose shipments or data could be affected.

contacts.role: Whoever set up our email and computers

scenarios.name: Ransomware shuts down operations
scenarios.description: Criminals lock your computers and demand payment, and your operations stop until you recover.

default: Someone opens a booby-trapped email, or an old computer never gets updates
Criminals lock every computer they can reach, backups included
You can't take orders, invoice, or run equipment
Days of lost business, plus a ransom demand
carrier: A dispatcher opens a fake invoice attachment
Ransomware locks dispatch, TMS, and billing computers
Trucks can't be dispatched and reefer loads sit at the dock
Spoiled cargo, missed delivery windows, and angry grocers
broker: Someone opens a fake rate confirmation
Ransomware locks your TMS and load records
You can't tender, track, or pay carriers
Loads miss appointments and shippers move their freight elsewhere
coldstorage: Ransomware locks inventory and temperature-monitoring computers
Product warms up with no alarm, and orders can't ship
Spoiled stock, and customers asking what else was affected

scenarios.name: Fake payment request or invoice fraud
scenarios.description: Someone impersonates a supplier, carrier, or your boss by email and redirects a payment to their own bank account.

default: A criminal sends an email that looks like it's from a supplier
It says their bank details have changed
Someone updates the details without calling to check
Your payment goes to the criminal and is usually gone for good
carrier: An email that looks like your fuel supplier or factoring company arrives
It says: 'our bank details changed, please update them'
Someone updates them without calling a number you already had
Your next payment, often tens of thousands, goes to criminals
broker: A 'carrier' emails new bank details just before payday
Nobody calls that carrier at a number on file
You pay the fake account, and the real carrier still wants paying
You pay twice, and the carrier stops hauling for you

scenarios.name: Stolen logins to online business tools
scenarios.phrase: stolen logins to your online tools
scenarios.description: Someone gets into your load board, accounting, banking, or fleet portal using a stolen or guessed password.

default: A staff password is reused, leaked, or guessed
Criminals log in to your banking or supplier websites as you
They change payment details, order goods, or copy data
The losses show up weeks later
carrier: The shared load board password leaks
Criminals log in as your company
They book loads in your name or change where your payouts go
Shippers blame you, and your reputation takes the hit
broker: A TMS or load board password leaks
Criminals post fake loads or copy your carrier list
They pose as you to carriers and shippers
Stolen freight gets tied to your company name

scenarios.name: Tampering with connected equipment
scenarios.description: Refrigeration, grain dryers, sensors, or cameras are disrupted or accessed remotely by someone who should not be there.

default: A vendor's remote access to your equipment is left on all the time
Someone uses it to get into your equipment controls
Refrigeration, dryers, or sensors are switched off or changed
Product is ruined before anyone notices
carrier: The refrigeration vendor's remote access is always on
Someone connects to your reefer or dock controls
Temperatures change and no alarm goes off
A trailer of produce spoils before delivery
coldstorage: The refrigeration vendor's remote access is always on
Someone connects to your freezer or room controls
Setpoints change overnight with no alarm
A room of product has to be thrown away

scenarios.name: A vendor or IT provider gets breached
scenarios.phrase: a breach at a vendor or IT provider
scenarios.description: Attackers get into your business through a company you trust, like your IT provider or an equipment vendor.

default: Your IT provider or a software vendor is compromised
The attackers use that company's access to reach you
They move around quietly for weeks
Ransomware or data theft that started somewhere else
carrier: Your TMS, ELD, or IT provider is breached
Attackers use its connection into your office
Dispatch and customer data is exposed
You're shut down, and you weren't even the target

scenarios.name: Losing data you cannot get back
scenarios.phrase: losing data you cannot get back
scenarios.description: Files, records, or accounting data are destroyed and there is no way to restore them.

default: A computer dies, is stolen, or gets locked by ransomware
There's no backup that actually works
Invoices, records, and customer lists are gone
Weeks of rebuilding, and some of it never comes back
carrier: The office computer with dispatch records and rate sheets dies
The only backup is an old USB drive
BOLs, proof of delivery, and invoices are gone
You can't bill for loads you already delivered

scenarios.name: Misuse of shared or leftover accounts
scenarios.phrase: misuse of shared or leftover accounts
scenarios.description: Shared logins or ex-employee accounts are used without anyone knowing who did it.

default: Several people share one login, or an ex-employee's account still works
Someone misuses it
The records can't show who did what
You can't prove what happened, or lock out just that person
carrier: Dispatchers share one login, and a driver who left still knows it
Someone books or changes loads with it
The logs just say 'dispatch'
You can't tell who did it, or lock out just them

scenarios.name: Load redirected to bad actors
scenarios.phrase: a load being redirected to bad actors
scenarios.description: Someone posing as your broker or customer asks for a new pickup or delivery address, one person changes it, and the load goes to bad actors.

default: Criminals get into a staff email account, or fake a customer's email
They see which shipments are worth the most
They ask for a 'new delivery address', and one person changes it
The load goes to bad actors
carrier: A dispatcher's email password is phished
Criminals read your shipment history and pick a high-value reefer load
Posing as the broker, they email a 'new delivery address'
One dispatcher changes it alone, and the load is gone
broker: Criminals phish your email or fake a shipper's
They pick a high-value load from your email threads
They send the carrier a 'revised' delivery address
The carrier delivers to bad actors, and you get the blame

impacts.label: Delayed or spoiled shipments to your customers
impacts.description: When your computers or equipment go down, loads sit at the dock, trucks cannot be dispatched, or cold goods warm up. Your customers get late or ruined product.

impacts.label: Fraudulent invoices sent to partners in your name
impacts.description: Criminals use your email or accounts to send fake invoices or bank-change requests to your customers and suppliers. They pay because it looks like it came from you.

impacts.label: Attackers reaching partners through shared systems
impacts.description: Shared portals, vendor connections, and email threads let an attacker who gets into your business move on into a partner's systems.

impacts.label: Customers' loads stolen or delivered to bad actors
impacts.description: A redirected or double-brokered load never reaches the grocer or processor waiting for it. They lose the product and the shelf space, and they remember whose truck it was.

impacts.label: Failed customer security audit
impacts.description: Grocers, processors, and shippers increasingly send suppliers security questionnaires. Gaps like these can fail them and put contracts at risk.

impacts.label: Partner and customer data exposed
impacts.description: Information partners trusted you with, like rates, contacts, or payment details, ends up in the wrong hands.

templates.name: CCCS baseline + CIS Controls
templates.tagline: The federal baseline, with the international CIS Controls alongside it.
templates.bestFor: Answering customer or insurer questionnaires, which often ask about CIS Controls.
reportsOn: CIS Controls v8.1 safeguards, including Implementation Group 1

templates.name: CyberSecure Canada (CAN/CIOSC 104)
templates.tagline: The national standard behind the CyberSecure Canada certification and the OCI Cybersecurity Workbook.
